Senses.Explanation: The inner chamber is what lies past a house’s public gate and hall; Chan records bend that architectural depth into the inner matter of the named teaching figure’s house, lineage formulations, or an encounter. An interlocutor asks whether two establishments differ in “public frontage and inner chamber,” making the outer/inner house contrast explicit. Wanan Daoyan says only one who enters the gateless gate can sit within the inner chamber. Sanfeng Hanyue Fazang calls Linji’s mysteries, essentials, guest, and host the inner matters differentiated within one phrase. Baiyu Jingsi says not to seek the inner chamber elsewhere; an unnamed monk says Zhaozhou’s walls admitted him and asks about the inner-chamber matter; Yingning Jing directs one who wants to enter deeply to inquire of an elder. The Zen bend preserves the spatial constraint—past frontage into the inside—while applying it to what is intimate or internal to a teaching house, without inventing a secret teaching formulation.

Senses.Explanation: The head-of-hall reverend is the monastery’s presiding abbot or teacher as named from the community’s institutional side. Pure rules put the title into invitations, announcements, and appointments: a formal notice invites a head-of-hall reverend, a hall attendant announces that he has cancelled evening interview, and a rector cites his instruction when appointing an officer. Reception language asks the head-of-hall reverend at Wuzu to expound before the assembly. Tianyi Yihuai credits the named teaching figure with close formation and encouragement, while Hongjue Min uses the title when announcing the death of the present monastery’s presiding teacher. The Chan bend is institutional rather than symbolic: the named teaching figure of public encounter is named here as the person who presides over the hall and whose word organizes its communal offices and events.

Senses.Explanation: To stand with one’s head against heaven and feet on earth is the record’s epithet for a person presented as fully standing on their own. Masters apply it to the person within a monastery’s scene, to traveling monks carrying staffs, and to the one who can withstand direct testing without retreating into excuses. Feiyin Tongrong answers “what is the person within Huangbo’s scene?” with “head against heaven and feet on earth,” making the phrase a direct portrait-answer. Lianfeng Su addresses the “superior one who investigates Chan” as iron-headed, copper-browed, and standing between heaven and earth before describing blows and reversals that do not move him. Sanyi Mingyu pairs the phrase with having neither a tile overhead nor room below for an awl, while an unnamed monk in Lingji Xingguan’s record uses it to challenge why so many people are buried alive. Juelang Daosheng makes the status conditional: only one who can pass through the successive shouts is allowed to be such a person. The phrase is therefore an epithet tested in public speech, not a physical measurement.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase pictures an extra eye at the crown of the head; speakers require, open, test, or attribute this eye in public encounters. The records use it with the verbs possess, open, look, illuminate, and strike blind, and with the adjective correct. Lushan Fazhen says that to understand the upward matter one must possess the crown-gate eye; possessing it accords with the heart of leaving home, and he then asks, “do you want to understand the crown-gate eye?” before saying that people in the four capitals put on clothes and eat while people in the two Zhejiang circuits are full and warm (欲明向上事，須具頂門眼；要會頂門眼麼？四京人著衣喫飯，兩浙人飽暖自如). Yuanwu invites “those who possess the crown-gate eye” to raise Xuansha's case (具頂門眼者，請試舉看), and says in verse that when the crown-gate eye is correct it has complete efficacy (頂門眼正有全功). Dahui says a flash of lightning opens the crown-gate eye (激電爍開頂門眼). In a direct exchange, the unnamed monk says the furnace has opened it; Chaozong Tongren asks what it is, the unnamed monk bows, and Chaozong Tongren strikes him and says, “it has been knocked blind” (擉瞎了也). A transmission record appraises Zhaozhou as possessing it while distinguishing black and white in a stone-struck spark (趙州具頂門眼，向擊石火裏分緇素). The term is repeatedly attested. Jifei Ruyi directly turns the image back into a public question, asking, “What is the eye at the crown?” This questioning use concerns the same eye-image, not another object.
